analysis.one_liner: Repeals the law requiring federal service contractors to pay workers prevailing wages and benefits.
analysis.headline: A House Republican bill to repeal the Service Contract Act never got a vote: it sat in committee from April 1993 until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Service Contract Act of 1965 requires companies that win federal service contracts — janitorial, security, food service, and similar work — to pay their workers government-set prevailing wages and benefits. This bill would have wiped that law off the books, letting contractors pay whatever the market would bear on future contracts. It was introduced by Rep. John Boehner with 15 Republican cosponsors, referred to the House Education and Labor Committee, sent to a subcommittee, and never acted on again.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal service contractors would gain, because wages and benefits for their lowest-paid workers are a large share of contract cost. Without the Act, bids could be built on lower pay, and contractors could undercut competitors who follow the wage floor. Company owners and shareholders would capture the savings on new contracts.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Service Contract Act of 1965 outright, removing the requirement that federal service contractors pay prevailing wages and benefits [S3].
It applies only to contracts entered into after enactment; contracts already signed would stay covered by the old rules [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The workers — janitors, security guards, food service workers, groundskeepers, and others employed by federal contractors — would bear the cost, as the wage and benefit floors that now apply to their jobs would disappear. Because the Act's wage determinations follow the work to whichever company wins the contract, repeal would let new contractors cut pay below what workers currently earn on those jobs.

drawbacks.text: Repeal would remove the only wage floor on federal service contracts, exposing roughly the lowest-paid tier of federally contracted workers to pay cuts whenever a contract changes hands [S2].

Supporters' main argument would be that the Act raises the price the government pays for services and burdens small contractors with compliance paperwork; repeal could lower contract costs for taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings to contractors and possibly to taxpayers come directly out of the paychecks of some of the lowest-paid workers on government jobs. The bill offered no replacement protection for those workers, so its benefit to business would be their loss in wages.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to a subcommittee, which never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Boehner introduced the bill on March 30, 1993, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor [S1] [S5].
On April 16, 1993, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor Standards, Occupational Health and Safety, where no further action was recorded [S5].
The bill had 15 cosponsors, all Republicans, and never reached the House floor for a vote [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal service contract workers are better off, because the wage and benefit protections of the Service Contract Act remained in force. Contractors who would have saved on labor costs did not get that saving.

for.name: Rep. John Boehner
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Service Contract Act.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, referred it to a subcommittee, and never reported it out, keeping it off the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 15 cosponsors were Republicans; the bill died without action in the Democratic-controlled Education and Labor Committee.

industries.industry: Federal service contractors (janitorial, security, food service, maintenance)
industries.note: This bill would have freed contractors from paying the government-set prevailing wages and benefits now required on federal service contracts, cutting their labor costs on new bids. Because those savings would come out of the pay of low-wage contract workers, the industry's gain in this bill ran against the workers' interest. The bill died, so contractors keep paying the wage floor.
